cues.text: A Priest Who Had Stopped Believing
Around the year 1300, in the small Benedictine monastery of O'Cebreiro , high in Galicia's mountains along the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela, a priest was assigned to celebrate Mass.
His own faith in the Real Presence had quietly eroded, and the morning's driving snow and freezing wind convinced him no one would come.
A Farmer Who Came Anyway
A farmer named Juan Santín , from the nearby hamlet of Barxamaior, made his way up through the blizzard regardless.
He arrived soaked and half-frozen to kneel in the cold stone church.
The priest, privately scornful of a man risking so much for what he inwardly considered no more than bread and wine, offered the Mass anyway, though without devotion.
Flesh and Blood at the Consecration
Immediately after the words of consecration, tradition holds, the Host visibly became flesh and the wine in the chalice became blood.
The blood overflowed, staining the corporal beneath it; both the priest and the farmer witnessed the transformation together.
The priest's own faith is said to have been restored on the spot.
A Queen's Reliquary
The relics remained on the altar for nearly two centuries until, tradition holds, Queen Isabella I of Castile learned of the miracle.
Passing through O'Cebreiro on pilgrimage to Santiago, she had a crystal reliquary made to hold the Host.
The earliest surviving documentary reference to the whole episode is a papal letter from 1487, nearly two centuries after the event itself, a gap this entry notes rather than glosses over.
Legacy
Tradition holds that the priest and Juan Santín are buried together beside the altar where the miracle occurred.
A wooden statue of the Virgin nearby, said to have inclined her head in adoration at the moment of consecration, is venerated today as the Virgen del Milagro .
The relics remain enshrined above the tabernacle in the Church of Santa María la Real.
They are carried each year in procession on the feast of Corpus Christi, on August 15, and on September 8.
This small mountain church is still passed through by pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago, much as one cold, unbelieving farmer once did.
